blocks.text: Sulfonamides are synthetic compounds derived from sulfanilamide, discovered by Gerhard Domagk in 1932. They treat bacterial infections, mainly urinary tract and skin infections, by inhibiting the bacterial synthesis of folic acid, which is essential for DNA synthesis and growth. They act as competitive inhibitors and are bacteriostatic. They are usually taken by mouth; side effects include rashes, nausea, sensitivity to light and kidney damage.

items: Bacteriostatic: they do not kill bacteria at once but stop their growth, so the immune system can destroy them.
Selective toxicity: bacteria must build folate themselves, while humans absorb it from food, so the drug starves bacteria of a vital nutrient and leaves human cells untouched.
Competitive inhibition: as look-alikes of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), they bind the bacterial enzyme that uses PABA to make folate, blocking the pathway.
Combined therapy: they are often combined with trimethoprim for a stronger, bactericidal effect.
Broad spectrum: they act against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and are used for urinary tract infections, acne and respiratory infections.
